title: Review: Experimental design and variables; Diet, energy balance and obesity indicators; Monosaccharides and disaccharides; Polysaccharides; Elements, monomers and condensation/hydrolysis
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM04#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM03#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM02#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM03#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM02#N.8a, BM03#N.7a, BM04#N.6, EX14a#N.4, EX14b#N.11, PR01b#N.12, BM02#N.10a, BM03#N.10a, BM04#N.13a, EX14b#N.8, PR01b#N.5, BM03#N.9. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Glycogen
items.clue: The energy store found in animals and fungi

items.label: Monosaccharide
items.clue: A single sugar unit: the building block of carbohydrates

items.label: Polymer
items.clue: A large molecule made of many small units joined together

items.label: Isomers
items.clue: Molecules such as glucose and fructose: same atoms, arranged differently

questions.stem: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?

options.text: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released
A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide
Water dissolves the two monomers so that they meet, but no water is formed or used

questions.explanation: An –OH from one monomer and an –H from the other combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers.

questions.stem: The enzyme maltase, in the small intestine, acts on maltose. Which statement describes the reaction?

options.text: Condensation: a glycosidic bond forms and a water molecule is released.
Hydrolysis: a hydrogen bond between two glucose molecules is broken.
Hydrolysis: a glycosidic bond is broken, using water, giving two glucose.
Hydrolysis: a glycosidic bond is broken, releasing water, giving two glucose.

questions.explanation: Maltose is glucose + glucose. One water is split; –H and –OH go to the two products.

questions.stem: Liver cells store glucose in the form of glycogen. Why is the glucose not simply stored as free glucose?

options.text: Glycogen is insoluble because it is non-polar, so it stays separate from the watery cytoplasm
The branches of glycogen make its glucose hard to remove, so the store is not used up too quickly
Glycogen is relatively insoluble because of its size, so it does not affect the osmotic balance of the cell
Glycogen stores extra energy in the glycosidic bonds that link its glucose monomers together

questions.explanation: Glycogen is very large and relatively insoluble, so much can be stored without raising the solute concentration of the cytoplasm. Free glucose would draw water in by osmosis.

questions.stem: A 40 g handful of mixed nuts contains 20 g fat, 6 g carbohydrate and 8 g protein. Using 37 kJ g⁻¹ for fat and 17 kJ g⁻¹ for carbohydrate and protein, what is its energy content?

options.text: 236 kJ
578 kJ
978 kJ

questions.explanation: Fat: 20 × 37 = 740 kJ. Carbohydrate and protein: (6 + 8) × 17 = 238 kJ. Total 978 kJ.

questions.stem: A male rugby player is 1.85 m tall with a mass of 105 kg. His waist is 88 cm and his hips are 104 cm. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: He is obese and at high CHD risk, because his BMI is above 30 and BMI measures body fat.
His WHR is 1.18, so he carries a lot of central fat.
His BMI is in the obese range, but his WHR (0.85) suggests little central fat.
Neither indicator gives useful information, because they give conflicting results here.

questions.explanation: BMI = 105 ÷ 1.85² = 30.7. WHR = 0.85, below the 0.90 threshold for men. Muscle may explain his high BMI. The indicators disagree, which is why neither is used alone.

questions.stem: A student uses a water bath to keep enzyme tubes at 30 °C. Her thermometer gives readings that agree closely: 30.0, 30.0, 30.5, 30.0 °C. A calibrated electronic probe in the same water bath reads 28.0 °C. Which improvement would make her temperature measurements more accurate?

options.text: Take ten readings with the same thermometer and use their mean.
Calibrate the thermometer against the probe, or use the probe instead.
Record each reading to two decimal places, so that the mean is more exact.
Calculate the range of her readings, to show that they are accurate.

questions.explanation: The readings are precise but about 2 °C high: a systematic error. Only calibration (or a calibrated instrument) brings the readings close to the true value.

questions.stem: A polypeptide made of 100 amino acids is completely hydrolysed into free amino acids. How many water molecules are used in the process?

options.text: 99 water molecules
100 water molecules
1 water molecule
0 water molecules

questions.explanation: 100 amino acids are joined by 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, split to supply the –H and –OH.

questions.stem: Galactose and glucose both have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and both form a ring of five carbons and one oxygen. They differ only in which way the –OH on carbon 4 points. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They are isomers: two hexoses with the same atoms arranged differently.
They must have different formulae, because they are different sugars.
They are α-glucose and β-glucose, the same sugar drawn in two different ways.
Galactose is a pentose, as only five carbons are in its ring.

questions.explanation: Same formula, different arrangement. Like glucose and fructose in the hook, that is enough to make a different sugar with a different shape.

questions.stem: Humans make amylase, which hydrolyses the 1,4-glycosidic bonds between α-glucose units in starch. Humans make no enzyme that hydrolyses cellulose, which also has 1,4-glycosidic bonds between glucose units. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Cellulose's glycosidic bonds are much stronger than those in starch, so amylase cannot break them.
Cellulose chains are coiled and branched, so amylase cannot reach the bonds.
Cellulose is non-polar, so it cannot dissolve and enzymes cannot act on it.
Its β-glucose units alternate in orientation, so its bonds have a different shape.

questions.explanation: Amylase only fits bonds between α-glucose units. In cellulose, alternate β-glucose units are flipped, so the bond looks different to an enzyme. Cows rely on gut microbes that make cellulase.

questions.stem: A survey finds that people who eat more fruit have lower rates of CHD. A headline says: "Fruit prevents heart disease." Which is the best response?

options.text: It is a correlation; fruit eaters may differ in other ways, such as smoking.
The claim is proven, because the survey included a very large number of people.
There can be no link, because fruit contains almost no fat or cholesterol.
The claim is proven, because fruit contains antioxidants such as vitamin C.

questions.explanation: Observational data cannot rule out other factors. For example, vitamin C supplements given at random in a large trial did not reduce cardiovascular events.

questions.stem: A potato cylinder's mass falls from 3.62 g to 3.40 g in a sucrose solution. The balance reads to ±0.01 g. What is the percentage error in the change in mass?
questions.explanation: Change = 3.62 − 3.40 = 0.22 g, uncertainty = 0.01 + 0.01 = ±0.02 g (OCR form: 2 × 0.01). Percentage error = 0.02 ÷ 0.22 × 100 = 9.1%. A small change carries a large percentage error.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly links a property of glucose to the way it is used in organisms?

options.text: Glucose breaks down readily on its own, which is why it is used as a respiratory substrate
Glucose is chemically stable, so it is transported in blood plasma without breaking down
Glucose dissolves in water because its molecules are small, so it is easily transported
Glucose is highly soluble, so cells store large quantities of it dissolved in their cytoplasm

questions.explanation: Glucose's bonds break only when enzymes act on it in respiration. This stability, with its solubility, lets it be carried in blood to the cells that oxidise it.
